### 1.  A construction (lower bound)

Take all subsets whose size is at most \(p+1\):

\[
\mathcal{F}_{0}= \{\,X\subseteq A:|X|\le p+1 \,\}.
\]

If \(X\neq Y\) are in \(\mathcal{F}_{0}\) then each of them has size \(\le p+1\);

and for smaller sets the intersection is even smaller.  Hence (1) holds.

The number of subsets in \(\mathcal{F}_{0}\) is  

\[
|\mathcal{F}_{0}|=\sum_{i=0}^{p+1}\binom{n}{i}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus  

\[
\max|\mathcal{F}|\ge \sum_{i=0}^{p+1}\binom{n}{i}.
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A useful observation

For any set \(X\) with \(|X|>p+1\) choose one of its \((p+1)\)-subsets,
for instance the lexicographically smallest \((p+1)\)-subset.
Define a mapping  

\[
\phi\colon\{X\in\mathcal{F}:|X|>p+1\}\longrightarrow\binom{A}{p+1},
\qquad 
\phi(X)=\text{chosen }(p+1)\text{-subset of }X .
\]

If two different sets \(X,Y\) satisfied \(\phi(X)=\phi(Y)=B\), then  
\(B\subseteq X\cap Y\) and \(|X\cap Y|\ge |B|=p+1\), contradicting (1).  
Hence \(\phi\) is **injective**.  Consequently  

\[
\bigl|\{X\in\mathcal{F}:|X|>p+1\}\bigr|
\;\le\;
\binom{n}{p+1}.
\tag{4}
\]

### 3.  Upper bound for any family

Separate the members of \(\mathcal{F}\) according to their size:

\[
\mathcal{F}= \underbrace{\{X\in\mathcal{F}:|X|\le p\}}_{\mathcal{F}_{\le p}}
\;\cup\;
\underbrace{\{X\in\mathcal{F}:|X|=p+1\}}_{\mathcal{F}_{p+1}}
\;\cup\;
\underbrace{\{X\in\mathcal{F}:|X|>p+1\}}_{\mathcal{F}_{>p+1}} .
\]

The three parts are disjoint, so

\[
|\mathcal{F}| = |\mathcal{F}_{\le p}|+|\mathcal{F}_{p+1}|+|\mathcal{F}_{>p+1}|.
\]

Obviously  

\[

\]

Putting the three estimates together gives

\[

\;\le\;
\sum_{i=0}^{p}\binom{n}{i}

\sum_{i=0}^{p+1}\binom{n}{i}.
\tag{5}
\]

\[
